L19: # API reference
L20: 
L21: Full HTTP API reference for the TypeSafe evaluation endpoint.
L22: 
L23: Copy page Copy page
L24: 
L25: Evaluate a `state` against a map of typed `questions` and get back structured `answers`, one per question. For a guided introduction, start with the cite3†primitives .
L26: 
L27: ##
L28: 
L29: cite4†​ L30: 
L31: Evaluation endpoint
L32: 
L33:     `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone
L34:     Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>
L35:     Content-Type: application/json
L36:     `
L37: ##
L38: 
L39: cite5†​ L40: 
L41: Request body
L42: 
L43: The top-level shape of every request. Each entry in the `questions` map is a typed question you name.
L44: 
L45: cite6†​ L46: 
L47: [Button: state]
L48: 
L49: string | object | array
L50: 
L51: required
L52: 
L53: The content to evaluate. A plain string for text, or structured data (object/array) for things like chat logs, records, or the current state of your application. See cite7†State for formats and best practices.
L54: 
L55: cite8†​ L56: 
L57: [Button: model]
L58: 
L59: string
L60: 
L61: required
L62: The model that handles the request. Use `"jev-latest"`, TypeSafe’s flagship model. See cite9†Models for the available models and aliases.
L63: 
L64: cite10†​ L65: 
L66: [Button: questions]
L67: 
L68: map<string, Question>
L69: 
L70: required
L71: 
L72: A map of typed cite11†Question objects. You choose each key; answers come back under the same keys.
L73: 
L74: Show map entries
L75: 
L76: cite12†​ L77: 
L78: [Button: ‹question id›]
L79: 
L80: Question
L81: 
L82: A key you choose. The matching cite13†Answer is returned under this same id. The key is not sent to the underlying model and is not used in inference.
L83: Example request
L84: 
L85:     `{
L86:       "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days.",
L87:       "model": "jev-latest",
L88:       "questions": {
L89:         "is_urgent": {
L90:           "type": "noul",
L91:           "instructions": "Does this convey urgency?"
L92:         }
L93:       }
L94:     }
L95:     `
L96: ##
L97: 
L98: cite11†​ L99: 
L100: Question types
L101: 
L102: A `Question` is one of three types, set by its `type` field. All three share `type` and `instructions`; each adds its own `criteria`.
L103: ###
L104: 
L105: cite14†​ L106: 
L107: Noul
L108: 
L109: A yes/no question. Returns the probability the answer is yes.
L110: 
L111: cite15†​ L112: 
L113: [Button: type]
L114: 
L115: "noul"
L116: 
L117: required
L118: 
L119: cite16†​ L120: 
L121: [Button: instructions]
L122: 
L123: string | object | array
L124: 
L125: required
L126: 
L127: The yes/no question to evaluate.
L128: 
L129: cite17†​ L130: 
L131: [Button: criteria]
L132: 
L133: object
L134: 
L135: Optional descriptions of what a yes and a no mean.
L136: 
L137: Show properties
L138: 
L139: cite18†​ L140: 
L141: [Button: true]
L142: 
L143: string
L144: 
L145: What a yes (value near 1) means.
L146: 
L147: cite19†​ L148: 
L149: [Button: false]
L150: 
L151: string
L152: 
L153: What a no (value near 0) means.
L154: Example request
L155: 
L156:     `{
L157:       "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days.",
L158:       "model": "jev-latest",
L159:       "questions": {
L160:         "is_urgent": {
L161:           "type": "noul",
L162:           "instructions": "Does this convey urgency?",
L163:           "criteria": {
L164:             "true": "Explicitly time-sensitive",
L165:             "false": "No urgency expressed"
L166:           }
L167:         }
L168:       }
L169:     }
L170:     `
L171: ###
L172: 
L173: cite20†​ L174: 
L175: Choice
L176: 
L177: Picks one option from a set you define. Returns the chosen option and the full probability distribution.
L178: 
L179: cite21†​ L180: 
L181: [Button: type]
L182: 
L183: "choice"
L184: 
L185: required
L186: 
L187: cite22†​ L188: 
L189: [Button: instructions]
L190: 
L191: string | object | array
L192: 
L193: required
L194: 
L195: What the model should decide.
L196: 
L197: cite23†​ L198: 
L199: [Button: criteria]
L200: 
L201: map<string, string | null>
L202: 
L203: required
L204: 
L205: A map of option to rubric description; use null when an option needs no extra detail.
L206: 
L207: Show map entries
L208: 
L209: cite24†​ L210: 
L211: [Button: ‹option›]
L212: 
L213: string | null
L214: A key you choose. A description of this option.
L215: Example request
L216: 
L217:     `{
L218:       "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days.",
L219:       "model": "jev-latest",
L220:       "questions": {
L221:         "department": {
L222:           "type": "choice",
L223:           "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
L224:           "criteria": {
L225:             "billing": "Payments, invoicing, refunds",
L226:             "technical": "Bugs, outages, integrations",
L227:             "sales": "Pricing, upgrades, new accounts"
L228:           }
L229:         }
L230:       }
L231:     }
L232:     `
L233: ###
L234: 
L235: cite25†​ L236: 
L237: Score
L238: 
L239: Rates the state along a rubric you define. Returns a probability-weighted value across your levels.
L240: 
L241: cite26†​ L242: 
L243: [Button: type]
L244: 
L245: "score"
L246: 
L247: required
L248: 
L249: cite27†​ L250: 
L251: [Button: instructions]
L252: 
L253: string | object | array
L254: 
L255: required
L256: 
L257: What the model should rate.
L258: 
L259: cite28†​ L260: 
L261: [Button: criteria]
L262: 
L263: array
L264: 
L265: required
L266: 
L267: An ordered array of level descriptions. You must include at least two levels.
L268: Example request
L269: 
L270:     `{
L271:       "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days.",
L272:       "model": "jev-latest",
L273:       "questions": {
L274:         "frustration": {
L275:           "type": "score",
L276:           "instructions": "How frustrated is the customer?",
L277:           "criteria": ["Calm", "Frustrated", "Very angry"]
L278:         }
L279:       }
L280:     }
L281:     `
L282: ##
L283: 
L284: cite29†​ L285: 
L286: Response body
L287: 
L288: One answer per question, returned under the same ids you provided.
L289: 
L290: cite30†​ L291: 
L292: [Button: model]
L293: 
L294: string
L295: 
L296: required
L297: 
L298: The model that performed the evaluation.
L299: 
L300: cite31†​ L301: 
L302: [Button: answers]
L303: 
L304: map<string, Answer>
L305: 
L306: required
L307: 
L308: One cite13†Answer per question, keyed by the same ids you used in questions.
L309: 
L310: Show map entries

L312: cite32†​ L313: 
L314: [Button: ‹question id›]
L315: 
L316: Answer
L317:

L320: cite33†​ L321:

L546: ##

L548: cite53†​ L549: 
L550: Errors
L551: 
L552: Errors use standard HTTP status codes with a JSON body describing what went wrong.
L553: Status  | Meaning
L554: --- | ---
L555: `401 Unauthorized`  | Missing or invalid API key. Check the `Authorization` header.
L556: `422 Unprocessable Entity`  | The request body failed validation — for example a missing required field or a malformed question. The body details the offending field.
L557: `429 Too Many Requests`  | You have exceeded your rate limit. Back off and retry after a short delay.
L558: `529 Overloaded`  | TypeSafe is temporarily overloaded. Retry after a short delay.
L559: ###
L560: 
L561: cite54†​ L562: 
L563: Handling rate limits
L564: 
L565: When you receive a `429 Too Many Requests` or `529 Overloaded` response, retry the request with exponential backoff instead of retrying immediately. Our client SDKs handle this automatically, so no extra handling is needed if you use one of our SDKs with its default retry policy.

Yes, Girl Dinner is a strong fit for Jev. The key is that Jev will make the judgment; it will not discover restaurants or fetch menus itself. We supply the current people, preferences, locations, and restaurant data as structured state, and Jev returns typed scores and probabilities that our code can rank.

### 1. How we’ll use Jev

Jev accepts:

- A `state`: text or structured JSON containing everything it should consider.
- One or more typed questions.
- The `jev-latest` model.

It supports three question types:

- **Score**: Rate something on levels we define.
- **Choice**: Select from a fixed set of options.
- **Noul**: Return the probability that a yes/no statement is true.

The response is structured data rather than generated prose. Score and Choice answers include probability distributions and confidence values. Questions sharing the same state can be evaluated together in one request. [Jev introduction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction), [question primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives), [API reference](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api).

For Girl Dinner, the flow should look like this:

1. Each person supplies cravings, dislikes, dietary restrictions, budget, travel preference, and location.
2. Normal code finds nearby restaurants and calculates distances or travel times.
3. We remove restaurants that fail hard rules such as being closed, too far away, or having no verified option for an allergy.
4. We send the remaining restaurants and party preferences to Jev.
5. Jev independently scores each restaurant against each person’s preferences and the overall group.
6. Our code combines those scores, accounting for both the average and the least-satisfied person.
7. If the top result has low confidence or two restaurants are nearly tied, Girl Dinner asks one focused follow-up question.

A simplified state would resemble:

```json
{
  "people": [
    {
      "id": "alex",
      "cravings": ["spicy", "noodles"],
      "dietaryRestrictions": ["vegetarian"],
      "budget": "$$"
    },
    {
      "id": "sam",
      "cravings": ["Thai", "something light"],
      "dietaryRestrictions": [],
      "budget": "$$"
    }
  ],
  "restaurants": [
    {
      "id": "restaurant_123",
      "cuisines": ["Thai"],
      "priceLevel": 2,
      "openNow": true,
      "travelMinutes": {
        "alex": 12,
        "sam": 9
      },
      "menuItems": [
        {
          "name": "Vegetable drunken noodles",
          "tags": ["vegetarian", "spicy"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

We would send narrow Score questions such as:

- How well does restaurant 123 match Alex’s current cravings?
- How well does restaurant 123 match Sam’s current cravings?
- How much appealing menu variety does restaurant 123 offer this party?
- How well does restaurant 123 fit the party’s requested dining experience?

Our code would normalize those answers and calculate a final rank. Jev’s documentation specifically recommends splitting broad judgments into atomic questions, asking them together, and combining their outputs in code. [How to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one).

Dietary allergies should be enforced as hard application rules using explicit menu or allergen data. Jev can help interpret fuzzy descriptions such as “something light,” but it should not be the final authority on whether a meal is medically safe.

For confidence, we can use a product behavior like:

- High confidence: show the recommendation.
- Medium confidence: show two finalists or ask one tie-breaking question.
- Low confidence: ask for more preference information.

That follows TypeSafe’s recommended confidence-gated approach. [Confidence documentation](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence).

For implementation, TypeSafe provides an official JavaScript/TypeScript SDK:

```bash
npm install @typesafe-ai/sdk
```

It requires Node.js 20 or newer, reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from the environment, and uses `jev-latest` by default. [Official JavaScript SDK](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-sdk-js).

### 2. What I need from you

The only credential we definitely need for Jev is a **TypeSafe API key**. It is not currently available in this workspace.

You’ll need to:

1. Sign in to the [TypeSafe console](https://console.typesafe.ai/settings/keys).
2. Create an API key.
3. Add it to the project as `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`.

Please don’t paste the key into chat or commit it to Git. Once we choose the application framework, we’ll put it in the appropriate local environment file and ensure that file is ignored. The key must stay on the server; the browser should call our server endpoint rather than TypeSafe directly.

I cannot independently generate that key because it belongs to your TypeSafe account and may involve login, accepting their terms, credits, or billing. I can handle all code and configuration after it has been provisioned.

For the complete product, we will probably also need:

- **Google Maps/Places credentials** for restaurant discovery, place details, maps, and possibly travel times. Google requires a Cloud project, an API key, enabled APIs, and billing. Nearby Search can return restaurants, locations, cuisine types, price information, ratings, hours, websites, and some dining attributes. [Google Places Nearby Search](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/nearby-search).
- **No key for device GPS itself.** Web browsers expose location through `navigator.geolocation`; each participant must grant permission. It requires HTTPS in production. [Browser geolocation guidance](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/geolocation).
- **A menu-data strategy.** Google Places does not provide complete structured restaurant menus. It can provide the restaurant website and some attributes, but not dependable item-by-item menu and allergen data. Yelp’s paid Places plans can provide a menu URL, but that still is not necessarily a structured menu feed. [Google Place fields](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/reference/rest/v1/places), [Yelp plan fields](https://docs.developer.yelp.com/page/start-your-free-trial).

My recommendation is to begin with Google Places for discovery and use restaurant metadata plus sample structured menus while we prove the Jev scoring workflow. Then we can choose a production menu source based on target launch cities and budget.

So, the immediate requirement from you is the TypeSafe API key. We can build the interface, data model, scoring architecture, and mocked restaurant flow before the Google key or menu provider is ready.

in the end would the users have multiple options maybe like tinder style that they can swipe through and then come to a final decision

Yes—that interaction fits the product very well. I’d use a Tinder-style card stack, with Jev deciding which options deserve to enter the stack and how they should be ordered.

Each card could show:

- Restaurant and cuisine
- Appealing menu items
- Price and travel time
- Dietary compatibility
- “Why it fits tonight”
- Photos and open/closed status

Users would swipe:

- Left: no
- Right: yes
- Up or a button: love it

For one person, the app learns from each swipe and narrows toward a final recommendation.

For groups, everyone swipes privately on the same shortlist. We combine their responses with Jev’s scores:

- A restaurant everyone likes becomes an immediate match.
- “Love” votes receive extra weight.
- Any hard rejection based on allergies or accessibility removes the restaurant.
- The algorithm avoids choosing something one person strongly dislikes simply because everyone else likes it.
- If several options remain close, the app presents a final two-option showdown.

When a winner appears, everyone gets a match screen such as:

> It’s a match: Thai tonight  
> 4 people liked it · 12-minute average trip · options for everyone

If the stack runs out, nobody agrees, or the final vote ties, the app transitions naturally:

> No restaurant match. It’s Girl Dinner time.

Then users swipe through light plates at home, such as a Mediterranean snack board, breakfast-for-dinner plate, or fruit-and-cheese plate. That keeps the interaction fun even when the restaurant decision fails.

The strongest flow is: **collect preferences → find eligible restaurants → Jev ranks the shortlist → everyone swipes → aggregate consensus → final match or Girl Dinner fallback**.

L19: # Primitives (Questions)
L20: 
L21: The three TypeSafe question types (Choice, Score, Noul), the typed answers they return, how to choose between them, and how to ask several at once.
L22: 
L23: Copy page Copy page
L24: TypeSafe’s primitives are the small, typed building blocks you compose in code. They come in pairs: a question defines one judgment for a cite3†System One model to make about a cite4†state , and its answer is the typed value that comes back. You compose the answers in your code to make decisions. There are three question types, each returning a different shape of answer.
L25: Type  | What it answers  | Returns
L26: --- | --- | ---
L27: cite5†Choice | Which of these options?  | `choice`, `probabilities`, `confidence`
L28: cite6†Score | Which level?  | `score`, `legend`, `probabilities`, `confidence`
L29: cite7†Noul | Is this true?  | `noul` (0 to 1)
L30: 
L31: You can ask one question or send several together. Every question in a request sees the same state, is evaluated independently, and returns a typed answer under the ID you chose.
L32: ##
L33: 
L34: cite8†​ L35: 
L36: Ask for one snap judgment per question
L37: System One models are built for fast, focused judgments. Ask for a judgment a knowledgeable person makes in a second given the right context. “Does this message convey urgency?” is a good question. “Analyze this message and determine the best course of action” is not. That needs slow reasoning, and it is a signal to break the task into small questions and compose the answers in code.
L38: If the judgment you want depends on several independent factors, ask about each factor separately and combine the answers with your own logic. Instead of “rate this startup pitch”, ask about market size, technical feasibility, and differentiation, then weight them in code based on their relative importance. When priorities shift, change the value of weights rather than rewriting a prompt. cite9†Ask multiple questions together shows how to do this.
L39: ##
L40: 
L41: cite10†​ L42: 
L43: Define a question
L44: 
L45: Every question has an ID, a `type`, and `instructions`. Choice and Score questions also take `criteria`, which define the options for a Choice question or the levels for a Score. Noul questions accept `criteria` as an optional clarification of what yes and no mean.
L46:   * ID. The key you pick, such as `refund_requested`. It identifies the answer in the response.
L47:   * `type`. One of `choice`, `score`, or `noul`.
L48:   * `instructions`. The question you are asking about the state. This is where your evaluation logic goes. Write it as a clear, specific question, or as a statement for the model to judge.
L49:   * `criteria`. The possible answers: a map of options for a Choice question, an ordered list of levels for a Score, and an optional description of yes and no for a Noul. Each question type’s page covers its shape.
L50: This question asks whether a customer requested a refund:
L51: 
L52:     `from typesafe_sdk import Noul
L53: 
L54:     questions = {
L55:         "refund_requested": Noul(
L56:             instructions="Does the customer request a refund?",
L57:         ),
L58:     }
L59:     `
L60: Question IDs are for your code. They are not sent to the model. Write the complete question in `instructions`, even when the ID seems self-explanatory.
L61: ##
L62: 
L63: cite11†​ L64: 
L65: Choose a question type
L66: 
L67: Pick the type that matches the shape of the answer you need.
L68:   * Choice fits when the answer is one of a known set of options with no order between them: routing a ticket to a department, classifying a document type, detecting a programming language. Give the full list of options, and add an `other` or `none of the above` option when the list might not cover every input.
L69:   * Score fits when the answer falls on a spectrum and you can describe what each point on that spectrum means: bug severity, customer frustration, skill level. The levels are yours to define, and the model returns a position along them.
L70:   * Noul fits a clean yes/no question where the probability itself is the useful signal: does this message report a bug, is the customer requesting a refund, does the resume mention distributed systems.
L71: Use Noul for a yes/no judgment and Score to measure a position on a spectrum. “Is this candidate strong in Python?” needs a clear definition of “strong”. A Noul value of 0.5 means the model gives yes and no equal probability. It does not mean the candidate has a medium skill level. An unclear definition makes that probability hard to interpret.If you want to measure skill level, use a Score with defined levels, such as no experience, some familiarity, daily use, and deep expertise.
L72: If you need a yes/no decision, define the condition clearly, such as “Does the resume state that the candidate has used Python at work?”
L73: If two types both seem to fit, prefer the one whose answer your code can act on directly. A Choice between `refund`, `rebook`, and `information` maps straight onto three code paths. A Score of customer frustration maps onto a threshold. A Noul maps onto an `if`.
L74: ##
L75: 
L76: cite12†​ L77: 
L78: What comes back
L79: 
L80: Answers are primitives too. Each question type returns a typed value that your code can compare, threshold, sort, pass into further logic, or put into the state of a follow-up request (see cite13†When one question depends on another ).
L81: Type  | Answer fields  | How to read it
L82: --- | --- | ---
L83: Choice  | `choice`, `probabilities`, `confidence`  | `choice` is the selected option. `probabilities` is the distribution across every option. `confidence` summarizes how peaked that distribution is.
L84: Score  | `score`, `legend`, `probabilities`, `confidence`  | `score` is a position along your levels, and can fall between two of them. `legend` repeats the levels by number. `probabilities` is the distribution across levels.
L85: Noul  | `noul`  | The probability that the answer is yes. Near 1 is a strong yes, near 0 a strong no, near 0.5 uncertain. Noul has no separate `confidence`.
L86: Two properties of these answers make them composable:
L87:   * Every answer is constrained to the options you supplied. The model returns a probability distribution over your options or levels, never a value outside them. Your code never has to recover a value from generated prose.
L88:   * Every answer is independent. One question’s answer is not hidden context for another. You can add or remove questions without changing the others’ results.
L89: cite14†Confidence explains how `confidence` is derived from `probabilities` and how to use it to decide when to act automatically and when to escalate to a person.
L90: ##
L91: 
L92: cite15†​ L93: 
L94: Reference specific fields
L95: The content being evaluated, the cite4†state , is often a JSON object with several parts: a conversation, a record, a policy. When a question is about one of those parts, name it in the `instructions` with a dot-and-index path to its key, including the backticks. The model then knows which part of the state to judge. Take the support conversation from the State page:
L96: 
L97:     `{
L98:       "ticket": {
L99:         "subject": "Duplicate charge",
L100:         "messages": [
L101:           {"from": "customer", "text": "I was charged twice for order A-104. Please refund the duplicate."},
L102:           {"from": "support", "text": "We are checking the charges."}
L103:         ]
L104:       },
L105:       "order": {
L106:         "id": "A-104",
L107:         "charges": [
L108:           {"amount_usd": 49, "status": "captured"},
L109:           {"amount_usd": 49, "status": "captured"}
L110:         ]
L111:       },
L112:       "refund_policy": "Duplicate charges are eligible for a refund."
L113:     }
L114:     `
L115: These two questions point at the customer’s message, the policy, and the charges by path:
L116: 
L117:     `questions = {
L118:         "refund_requested": {
L119:             "type": "noul",
L120:             "instructions": "Does `ticket.messages[0].text` request a refund?",
L121:         },
L122:         "policy_supports_refund": {
L123:             "type": "noul",
L124:             "instructions": (
L125:                 "Does `refund_policy` support the refund requested "
L126:                 "in `ticket.messages[0].text`, given `order.charges`?"
L127:             ),
L128:         },
L129:     }
L130:     `
L131: Explicit paths make it clear which parts of a structured state should inform each judgment. See cite4†State for how to structure the input.
L132: ##
L133: 
L134: cite9†​ L135: 
L136: Ask multiple questions together
L137: Send every question that uses the same state in one request. You can mix question types freely. System One models evaluate every question in a request in parallel. Adding questions barely changes the response time and costs only the tokens for the extra questions, which are cheap. Asking a question you might not need is close to free. This request classifies a customer message, checks for urgency, and scores frustration all at once: Our cite16†client SDKs provide typed questions and answers.
L138: In Python, pass a `questions` dictionary of `Choice`, `Noul`, and `Score` objects to `client.system_one(...)`. This request sends a ticket and a refund policy once and gets a typed answer for each question:
L139: 
L140:     `from typesafe_sdk import Choice, Noul, Score, TypeSafeClient
L141: 
L142:     state = {
L143:         "ticket_message": "My flight was cancelled. Can I get a refund?",
L144:         "refund_policy": "Cancelled flights are eligible for a full refund.",
L145:     }
L146: 
L147:     with TypeSafeClient() as client:
L148:         response = client.system_one(
L149:             state=state,
L150:             questions={
L151:                 "refund_requested": Noul(
L152:                     instructions="Does `ticket_message` request a refund?",
L153:                 ),
L154:                 "request_type": Choice(
L155:                     instructions="What is the main request in `ticket_message`?",
L156:                     criteria={
L157:                         "refund": "The customer wants money returned.",
L158:                         "rebooking": "The customer wants a replacement flight.",
L159:                         "information": "The customer is asking for information only.",
L160:                     },
L161:                 ),
L162:                 "frustration": Score(
L163:                     instructions="How frustrated does the customer appear in `ticket_message`?",
L164:                     criteria=[
L165:                         "Calm and neutral.",
L166:                         "Concerned but civil.",
L167:                         "Very angry or using strong language.",
L168:                     ],
L169:                 ),
L170:             },
L171:         )
L172: 
L173:     print(response.answers["refund_requested"].noul)
L174:     print(response.answers["request_type"].choice)
L175:     print(response.answers["frustration"].score)
L176:     `
L177: See cite16†client SDKs for installation and usage in your language.
L178: ###
L179: 
L180: cite17†​ L181: 
L182: Ask speculative questions
L183: Ask every question your code might need, including ones whose answer only matters for some inputs, and let the code decide which answers to use. If a ticket turns out not to be a bug report, ignore the severity answer. We call this the cite18†Speculative fan-out pattern. The cite19†Parallel questions cookbook shows how batching 13 questions into one call is 11.5x cheaper and 9.6x faster than 13 separate calls, with no change in the answers.
L184: The number of questions in one request is limited only by the request’s token budget, which the state and the questions share. The budget is around 32,000 tokens, roughly 150,000 characters of English text.
L185: Coding agents fall into the one question per call habit more than people do. The cite20†TypeSafe agent skill tells your agent to put many questions in each call, including ones that only matter for some inputs.
L186: ###
L187: 
L188: cite21†​ L189: 
L190: Split a complex judgment into several questions
L191: A judgment that depends on several things is best split into one question per thing. Combine the answers in your code, giving each a weight for its relative importance. The weights are yours. When the combined result doesn’t match what your team would decide, change them in code and run again. Adding questions barely changes the response time because they run in parallel within one request. The split costs a few extra question tokens.
L192: For example, ticket priority might be built from three Score questions: how severe the bug is, how frustrated the customer is, and how much the report gives an engineer to work with. The Score page walks through this request and the code that normalizes and weights the answers in cite22†Splitting a complex judgment into several Scores . This technique is called the cite23†Composite scoring pattern.
L193: ###
L194: 
L195: cite13†​ L196: 
L197: When one question depends on another
L198: Questions in the same request are independent: one answer does not become context for another question. If a later judgment depends on an earlier answer, make a second request in code. The dependency is real only when your code cannot build the second request until it has the first answer: it needs the answer to fetch more data for the state, to decide what the state is made of, or to pick the next question’s options. Otherwise, ask the questions together and combine their answers in code.
L199: Two requests are the exception, not the rule. If the second request’s questions could have been asked against the original state, ask them in the first request and let the code ignore the ones it doesn’t need. Three cookbooks make a second request for a real reason. cite24†Skill suggestion ranks 182 skills in one request, then fetches the full text of the top three and judges them again against that better evidence.
L200: cite25†Structure recovery asks whether each line break split a sentence, merges lines into blocks from those answers, then classifies the blocks, which did not exist until the first request had answered. cite26†Hierarchical classification uses each Choice answer to decide which options the next request offers. See cite27†How to build with TypeSafe for guidance on breaking a workflow into focused judgments.

L19: # Confidence
L20: 
L21: How TypeSafe reports certainty, how it differs from probability, and how to use it to control system behavior.
L22: 
L23: Copy page Copy page
L24: All Score and Choice answers from TypeSafe include a `probabilities` property representing the probability distribution across the options (for Choice) or levels (for Score). The shape of that distribution is what tells you how certain the model is: concentrated on one outcome means a confident answer, spread out means an uncertain one. The answer’s `confidence` property collapses that shape into a single number from 0 to 1, so you can threshold on it without doing the math yourself.
L25: (Noul answers don’t carry one.)
L26: ##
L27: 
L28: cite3†​ L29: 
L30: Confidence is derived from the probabilities
L31: 
L32: `confidence` is a statistic computed from the probability distribution the answer already gives you. TypeSafe computes it for you and returns it on every Choice and Score answer, so the common case needs no extra work on your side.
L33: A solid default: We provide `confidence` as a convenient measure that fits most use-cases, but you are never locked into our definition. Depending on what you are evaluating, a different measure may serve you better, which is exactly why we give you the full `probabilities` in the response. The pros and cons of different computations is a specialized topic that we’ll keep to a separate cookbook rather than this page, and will add the link here when we do!
L34: For a cite4†Choice , the distribution is `probabilities` across your options. For a cite5†Score , it is the distribution across your levels. In both cases a flatter distribution means lower confidence: low confidence on a Choice often means none of the options are a clear winner over the others, and low confidence on a Score often means the levels are ambiguous, multi-dimensional, or the state doesn’t contain enough to go on.
L35: ##
L36: 
L37: cite6†​ L38: 
L39: ”I don’t know” is a useful signal
L40: 
L41: If an intelligent system, whether human or machine, cannot express honest uncertainty, the system cannot be trusted. Confidence gives you a built-in mechanism for the model to say “I’m not sure about this one.” This lets your code implement different behavior for different levels of certainty, which is the foundation for building systems you can actually rely on.
L42: ##
L43: 
L44: cite7†​ L45: 
L46: Three paths for using confidence in your code
L47: A useful starting pattern is to divide confidence into three ranges, each producing a different system behavior: High confidence: Act automatically. The model has a clear read and you can proceed without human involvement. Medium confidence: Proceed with caution. The model has a reasonable answer but is not certain. Depending on context, you might ask the user to confirm, flag for review, or gather more information before acting. Low confidence: Do not act.
L48: Route to a human, request clarification, or fall back to a different system. The model is telling you it does not have enough information or the question is not a good fit. Where you draw those boundaries depends on the stakes.
L49: ##
L50: 
L51: cite8†​ L52: 
L53: Thresholds scale with risk
L54: A confidence threshold is not one number. Different actions within the same system should be gated at different levels depending on the consequences of getting it wrong.
L55: 
L56:     `response = client.system_one(
L57:         state=user_message,
L58:         questions={
L59:             "action": Choice(
L60:                 instructions="What is the user trying to do?",
L61:                 criteria={
L62:                     "check_balance": "View account balance",
L63:                     "approve_transfer": "Approve the pending withdrawal request",
L64:                     "support": "Get help with an issue",
L65:                 },
L66:             ),
L67:         },
L68:     )
L69: 
L70:     action = response.answers["action"]
L71:     confidence = action.confidence
L72: 
L73:     if confidence < 0.5:
L74:         # Model is genuinely unsure. Don't guess.
L75:         route_to_human(user_message)
L76: 
L77:     elif action.choice == "check_balance":
L78:         # Low stakes. Showing the wrong screen is recoverable.
L79:         show_balance(account_id)
L80: 
L81:     elif action.choice == "approve_transfer":
L82:         if confidence > 0.9:
L83:             # High stakes, high confidence. Proceed with confirmation.
L84:             confirm_then_execute(account_id)
L85:         else:
L86:             # High stakes, moderate confidence. Verify first.
L87:             ask_user_to_confirm(account_id)
L88:     `
L89: The 0.5 confidence floor catches anything the model reports as genuinely uncertain. Above that, the threshold for acting without confirmation is higher for a destructive operation than for a read-only one. Your code encodes the risk tolerance.
L90: 
L91: The correct threshold values depend on your domain and the performance of the model for your use case. Start with conservative thresholds, test with your own data, and adjust as you observe results.

L19: # Patterns
L20: 
L21: Architectural patterns for building systems with TypeSafe.
L22: 
L23: Copy page Copy page
L24: 
L25: TypeSafe is designed to sit within a larger system, powering decisions with AI. Learning to think in terms of discrete, atomic decisions that compose into complex system behavior is a key skill for getting the most out of TypeSafe. This section assumes you know the cite3†TypeSafe primitives and understand cite4†how confidence works . If not, read those first.

L20: # Quick start
L21: 
L22: Prefer to just dive in? Here’s everything you need to get started immediately.
L23: 
L24: Copy page Copy page
L25: ##
L26: 
L27: cite3†​ L28: 
L29: Try it: the Playground
L30: 
L31:   1. Open the cite4†Playground†console.typesafe.ai and log in.
L32:   2. Paste any text as the state.
L33: 
L34: Sample state
L35: 
L36:     `Hi, I've been trying to connect my Stripe account for 3 days and it keeps failing. I'm losing sales. Please help ASAP.
L37:     `
L38: 
L39:   3. Add a question. Try a Noul question: `"Does this message express urgency?"`
L40: 
L41:     `{
L42:       "urgency": {
L43:         "type": "noul",
L44:         "instructions": "Does this message express urgency?"
L45:       }
L46:     }
L47:     `
L48:   4. Add more questions. Mix Noul, Choice, and Score in one call and see all results at once.
L49: ##
L50: 
L51: cite5†​ L52: 
L53: Call it: the API
L54: 
L55:   1. Get your API key from the cite6†dashboard†console.typesafe.ai L56:   2. Make a POST request to the API endpoint

L160: cite11†​ L161: 
L162: Code it: the Python SDK
L163: 
L164:   1. Install the SDK (requires Python >= 3.10).
L165: 
L166: With pip
L167: 
L168:     `pip install typesafe-sdk
L169:     `
L170: 
L171: With uv
L172: 
L173:     `uv add typesafe-sdk
L174:     `
L175:   2. Use the SDK. The client reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from the environment and calls `jev-latest` by default.
L176: 
L177:     `from typesafe_sdk import Choice, Noul, Score, TypeSafeClient
L178: 
L179:     client = TypeSafeClient()
L180: 
L181:     ticket = "Hi, I've been trying to connect my Stripe account for 3 days and it keeps failing. I'm losing sales. Please help ASAP."
L182: 
L183:     response = client.system_one(
L184:         state=ticket,
L185:         questions={
L186:             "department": Choice(
L187:                 instructions="Which team should handle this",
L188:                 criteria={
L189:                     "billing": "Payment or subscription issues",
L190:                     "technical": "Bugs or integration problems",
L191:                     "sales": "Pricing or account questions",
L192:                 },
L193:             ),
L194:             "frustration": Score(
L195:                 instructions="How frustrated the customer appears",
L196:                 criteria=[
L197:                     "Calm, just stating facts",
L198:                     "Frustrated but civil",
L199:                     "Very angry, strong language",
L200:                 ],
L201:             ),
L202:             "is_urgent": Noul(
L203:                 instructions="The message conveys urgency or time-sensitivity",
L204:             ),
L205:         },
L206:     )
L207: 
L208:     print(response.answers["department"].choice)  # "billing"
L209:     print(response.answers["frustration"].score)  # 1.035
L210:     print(response.answers["is_urgent"].noul)     # 0.999
L211:     `

L19: # How to build with TypeSafe
L20: 
L21: Design AI-powered software by keeping code in control and giving System One narrow, structured decisions.
L22: 
L23: Copy page Copy page
L24: 
L25: System One is TypeSafe’s model for building AI-powered software, not agents. It does not generate code or choose its own next action. It provides AI primitives that embed into software, so code remains in control while the model handles common-sense judgments over unstructured data.
L26: Summary: build a normal software workflow and insert System One only where AI is needed.
L27: 
L28:   * Keep control flow, deterministic rules, and side effects in code.
L29:   * Break broad judgments into narrow, typed questions with explicit instructions and criteria.
L30:   * Give each question only the context it needs.
L31:   * Use probabilities and confidence to act, ask for review, or escalate.
L32:   * Ask independent questions together, then compose their answers in code.
L33: ##
L34: 
L35: cite3†​ L36: 
L37: Three software architectures
L38: 
L39: TypeSafe is designed for building AI-powered software, where code owns the workflow and AI handles narrow, structured decisions.
L40: 
L41:   * Traditional software
L42: 
L43:   * LLM agents
L44: 
L45:   * AI-powered software
L46: 
L47: Traditional code is a complex decision tree made from simple software primitives. Because each primitive is reliable, developers can compose them into higher-level abstractions.
L48: An agent processes instructions and chooses its next step. This works well when a person is monitoring the process, but every loop introduces another opportunity to go off the rails.
L49: 
L50: Code handles deterministic work and owns the control flow. The model appears only where the system needs programmable common sense or needs to interpret unstructured data. Each AI task is kept atomic and constrained.
L51: cite4†Image: Traditional software, agents, and AI-powered software shown as three different system architectures.†mintcdn.com cite5†Image: Traditional software, agents, and AI-powered software shown as three different system architectures.†mintcdn.com L52: ##
L53: 
L54: cite6†​ L55: 
L56: What makes System One composable
L57: 
L58: ## Structured
L59: 
L60: System One is type-safe by construction. Decisions and probabilities conform to the structured software types and JSON schema your code expects, so it never has to recover a value from generated prose.
L61: 
L62: ## Parallel
L63: 
L64: Questions are evaluated independently and in parallel. One primitive’s result does not become hidden context that changes another primitive’s result.
L65: ## Comparable
L66: 
L67: Outputs are sortable and can drive smart `if` statements, thresholds, and comparisons.
L68: 
L69: ## Fast
L70: 
L71: Most queries complete in about 100 ms. System One is fast enough for real-time request paths and user interfaces.
L72: 
L73: ## Calibrated confidence
L74: 
L75: cite7†RLCD communicates uncertainty through calibrated probabilities instead of tending toward overconfidence.
L76: ## Self-consistent
L77: 
L78: System One is designed to return stable answers across repeated evaluations. See the cite8†self-consistency cookbook .
L79: 
L80: Because every output is constrained to the supplied options, the model returns a full probability distribution over those options rather than inventing a value outside the schema. TypeSafe’s target is a greater than 100× intelligence-to-speed-and-cost ratio; the underlying bet is that cheaper intelligence will create much more demand.
L81: ##
L82: 
L83: cite9†​ L84: 
L85: Design a System One workflow
L86: 
L87: 1
L88: 
L89: ### Use code when you can
L90: 
L91: Keep deterministic work in code. It is reliable and cheap. Avoid agent `while` loops when a software workflow can express the same behavior.
L92: 
L93: Example: keep deterministic rules in code
L94: 
L95:     `days_overdue = (today - invoice.due_date).days
L96: 
L97:     if days_overdue > 30:
L98:         route_to_collections(invoice)
L99:     `
L100: 
L101: Browse the cite10†System One patterns for bounded ways to compose model decisions with code.
L102: 
L103: 2
L104: ### Decompose the input state
L105: 
L106: Include only the context relevant to the current questions. This helps the model avoid distractions and context rot. Do not rely on knowledge stored in model weights when current information can come from your own knowledge base.
L107: 
L108: Example: send only relevant context
L109: 
L110: 3
L111: ### Use structure in the input state
L112: 
L113: Use nested JSON for the `state` and `questions` fields. Point questions at specific values when that removes ambiguity, and include the backtick characters around each path inside the question.
L114: 
L115: Example: reference a nested value
L116: 
L117: Use a backticked dot-and-index path to point a question at a specific nested value, such as `support.tickets[0].message`.
L118: 
L119: 4
L120: ### Decompose the questions
L121: 
L122: Ask the most explicit, narrow, specific, atomic questions you can. Break down complex or ill-defined questions into separate questions that each evaluate one property.
L123: 
L124: This is probably the most important concept in this guide. Broad questions hide several judgments behind one answer. Atomic questions expose those judgments so you can inspect, tune, and combine them in code.
L125: 
L126: Example: decompose spam detection
L127: 
L128: Example: verify a tool-call trace
L129: 
L130: 5
L131: ### Use structure in the questions
L132: 
L133: Keep atomic questions short. When instructions or criteria need several kinds of guidance, use objects or arrays with named fields instead of flattening everything into a dense prose string. This makes the decision boundary easier to scan, review, and tune.For a Choice, describe what belongs in each option, what belongs in a neighboring option instead, and a few representative examples. Use the same field names across options so the model can compare them directly.
L134: Example: define contrastive Choice criteria
L135: 
L136: A short, unambiguous question or criterion can remain a string. Add structure when it separates guidance that would otherwise blur together. For the full set of places structure is accepted, and worked examples for instructions, Choice options, Score levels, and Noul criteria, see cite11†Advanced: structure .
L137: 
L138: 6
L139: ### Ask a lot of questions
L140: 
L141: Ask many narrow, independent questions about the same state in one request. This is how you maximize effectiveness and intelligence per dollar with the API: questions run in parallel, and code can combine their signals without adding serial model round trips.See the cite12†Speculative Fan-Out pattern and cite13†Parallel questions cookbook .
L142:

For Girl Dinner, our code will gather people, GPS, restaurant, and menu data; Jev will evaluate many small preference and fit questions in parallel; our code will combine those scores and enforce hard dietary rules. # Introducing System One Models and Jev

Diogo Almeida, founder, TypeSafe

Models have been superhuman at chat for years, so where is all the automation?

This has been my driving question for the last four years. At OpenAI, I helped build the methods that made language models useful at following instructions and talking with people. That work ended up as the research behind ChatGPT.  At the time, I thought maybe chat models would lead to AGI, but despite the hype it became obvious to me that there was something really big missing.

After two years in stealth, countless technical challenges, and research breakthroughs… I am beyond excited to announce that today, TypeSafe AI is releasing our first System One Model: a new class of frontier models built to make fast, structured decisions that software can use directly.

We built a new stack entirely focused on automation: with a new model architecture, parallel sampler for maximum efficiency, and training method we call Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD).

Our first public model is Jev, available today in early access. Jev achieves similar levels of intelligence on System One tasks compared to existing LLMs, while being two orders of magnitude faster and more efficient. While Jev gives up string generation, it’s optimized for structured outputs and can’t hallucinate. 

Think of Jev as a frontier-intelligence function call: unstructured state in, typed probabilistic decisions out. 

Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence so see below for the receipts. 💅

## Frontiers, Old and New

 | Existing LLMs  | System One + Jev
--- | --- | ---
Optimized with  | Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) / Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)  | Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD)
Optimizes for  | Human preference: writeups and chat responses that human raters prefer.
Verifiable rewards: outputs that can be programmatically verified.  | Calibrated decisions: answers with epistemically honest probabilities on System One tasks.
Inputs  | Unstructured data (e.g. text) with an emphasis on sequential messages.  | Unstructured data (e.g. text) with an emphasis on structured program state.
Outputs  | Strings / generated text. Strings are flexible and can be anything: chat responses, code, hallucinations, refusals, or even type-safe structured values. To be used by software, responses need to be parsed + validated. There is also always some risk that the AI goes off the rails.  | Type-safe structured values. Possible outputs and structure are defined in advance. The model never makes type errors. All answers are accompanied with calibrated probabilities and confidence scores.
Sampling  | Sequential. Generates one token at a time, each conditioned on the last.  | Parallel. Generates all outputs in a single query. Incredibly efficient and hardware-aware.
Cost  | Input tokens: from $0.20 to $10 / MTok.
Output tokens: ~5x more expensive than input tokens.  | Input tokens: $0.042 / MTok ($42 per billion tokens).
Output tokens: FREE (too cheap to meter).
Speed  | End-to-end response time is 3 to 329 seconds for frontier models.  Fast enough for interfacing with humans, but a big bottleneck when integrated in code.  | End-to-end response time is 70ms-500ms for TypeSafe. This can range from 40x-200x faster for the same levels of frontier intelligence for System One shaped queries.
Confidence  | Even if prompted for a confidence estimate, models tend to be overconfident and inconsistent. If a model can do a task 95% of the time but doesn’t say when it’s in the 5%, it can’t automate that task.  | Always communicates confidence and uncertainty with every output. Calibrated: higher confidence means higher accuracy. More consistent: returns similar answers for similar inputs.
Use cases  | Human-in-the-loop tasks (chatbots, copilots, coding agents). General and powerful, but requires human oversight because their freedom also means they might go off the rails.
Verifiable problems (math proofs, kernel optimization). When correctness can be checked cheaply and automatically, LLMs can generate, test, and iterate until they find something that works.
Demos. The flexibility of strings allows it to be incredible for quickly making prototypes that only work sometimes.  | AI-Powered Workflows / smart if-statements. Structured outputs slot into ordinary software as fuzzy decision rules: classify, route, score, extract, or branch where hand-written logic is too brittle. The surrounding code constrains their freedom, making them easier to compose into reliable systems.
Map-reducing over big data. Turn petabytes of data into features and insights.
Real-time applications. 100ms speeds means you can use AI in your applications where UX is critical.
Verify everything. Score, judge, verify, guardrail, and detect jailbreaks of LLM prompts, reasoning traces, and/or outputs.

## Evidence / Technical Results

We love skeptics, and are skeptics ourselves.

There are some claims you can easily verify:

  * Speed per call: We truly are that fast, though our published evals are generally run from our laptops on the West Coast (this is where our service is currently based).

  * Cost per call: We make our pricing transparent. We can’t prove it isn’t subsidized; we’ll need the long-term to prove the sustainability of our pricing (which we expect to go down, not up).

  * No type errors: This would be an easy thing to falsify with just a single counter-example, but it is mathematically impossible.

For our bolder claims, we want to provide as much nuance as we can.

### Side-by-side demonstration

Our side-by-side demo shows a key difference between our models and LLMs: Jev outputs all probabilities in parallel instead of autoregressively generating by token. Strings are extremely powerful and general, but costly. “Giving up” strings actually gives us a lot of superpowers!

Nuance:

  * For people with early access to TypeSafe, here is the actual query.

    * The query is highly simplified and `questions` were chosen to have descriptive, human-readable keys so that the output on the screen is understandable.

    * The `state` is also a short, dense, and detailed paragraph, to emphasize the difference in sampling methodology. The relatively shorter input paints our model in an advantageous light.

  * For the keen eyed, for the recorded run, the only disagreement with GPT-5.6 Terra is on “Churn likelihood level”. The actual answer seems genuinely ambiguous to us.

  * We used GPT-5.6 Terra with default reasoning for this example, because we’ve found it to be the most comparable at intelligence to Jev on average.

  * Fun fact: a similar demo was what convinced us to go all-in in the direction of System One Models!

### Workflow evals

We made a new type of evaluation to measure how well AI works within code. We don’t optimize for a ground truth classification orand allow the harness and model to change (potentially allowing for overfitting via harness engineering). Instead, we assume there is a correct compute graph (a “workflow” represented in code) and use the predictions of the largest, smartest, and most expensive external models as reference probabilities.

Rephrased: every model gets the same workflow. We test how they compare to the average of the smartest models (in this case, Astra and Fable).

Image

Jev is off the charts – owning the Pareto frontier for almost 2 orders of magnitude. We also compare to models with a generated prompt doing all the logic in their chain-of-thought, but this tends to do significantly worse than using the workflow itself.

Note that the calls here are significantly more complex than the side-by-side demonstration above. That’s because they’re more representative of the types of production workloads needed for true business automation. Below is the simplest of the 4 workflows we’re publishing:

Image

The most reliable real-world workflows tend to have many independent, decomposed questions, with fine-grained behavior that’s dependent on probabilities instead of discrete decisions. The end result is discrete branching, but how we get to a final answer involves a lot of domain-specific engineering that needs to be done highly consistently.

See our workflow evals site for all the details: examples, disagreements, full queries, and each workflow.

Nuance:

  * This is where the claims of 193.6x faster, 444.6x cheaper on our home page comes from, and we expect that these are on the higher end of real world gains.

  * These content of these workflows were not deliberately chosen nor constructed to make our model look good, and are not in our training distribution. However, they were made by individuals on our model capabilities team, so some bias could exist.

  * We use the average of GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 as the reference answer, which biases answers towards OpenAI and Anthropic’s models. We likely underestimate the relative performance of our model and DeepSeek’s models.

  * The LLMs use our System One LLM wrapper, which constrains LLMs to output structured decisions compatible with our API. We have found this to be the most accurate way to get decisions from LLMs, but this tends to be slower and more expensive than giving decisions without probabilities.

### Hallucination and Type-safety

Image

Hallucination and type-safety are intrinsically related, and we think the latter is table stakes for automation. Having a hallucinated tool call is inconvenient in an agent, but is an absolute deal-breaker if it’s part of a system with latency guarantees or it’s buried several layers deep in a dependency chain. Existing models, no matter how smart, still hallucinate and have type errors.

Nuance:

  * The numbers for LLMs are from OpenRouter i.e., there almost certainly is bias here: more complex queries might be routed to better models.

  * Our number is not empirical. Schema matching is guaranteed, thus we can confidently add 0% into the plots.

### Fun Demos

Perhaps the most exciting part of our work is enabling new use cases. We have a lot more to show you, but here are a couple of the team’s favorites:

#### Doom

We love how this doomo doomonstrates real-time intelligence and what can be doone with code + AI. The engineer behind it was worried about making 10 queries a second (which ends up costing ~$7/hour), but the rest of us agreed that was lower than expected! This is so fun we intend to not only release an in-depth walkthrough, but also host some events to hack on this.

Nuance:

  * The demo is on structured state as a data structure with text, not on images (yet…)

  * A non-AI doom bot could play better, but we wanted a bot that was reactive to different representations of game state, and most importantly… following instructions was cool as heck!

#### Wikiracing

The objective of the game is to start on one Wikipedia page and reach a specific other Wikipedia page using only links you come across while traversing. Each step can mean choosing between hundreds to thousands of links! It’s a great playground for demonstrating not just intelligence-per-second, but also the compounding benefits of not hallucinating with high-cardinality choices.

Nuance:

  * As far as we know, it was completely random that both the 2nd and 3rd challenges started with “Rubber Duck.” The author only noticed when the team pointed it out.

  * Our speedups here tend to be a lot less than in previous demos. That’s because this is against the non-reasoning modes of the models (except Astra which was set to the lowest reasoning setting). This is also why Jev tended to finish in fewer steps (a sign of greater intelligence). This was to make the demo more bearable to watch. The LLMs look much worse at this task than with reasoning enabled.

  * Jev supports a cardinality up to 255. For the higher cardinality choices, we do a 2 stage-system of scoring independently then making an explicit choice, hence the occassional slowdown.

## What’s next

We’re still in Jev’s early days. We have a lot more in the pipeline and are so excited to keep on shipping 🔥.

Today, we are opening early access and bringing developers off the waitlist as quickly as we can. We want to hear which decisions you need to automate, where Jev works, and where it falls short. Tell us what sci-fi you want to build!!

We started TypeSafe because we believe that AI needs an interface software could depend on. We can't wait to see new use cases continuously diffuse through the community and economy.

### We Give A FAQ

Where do the names “System One Models” and “Jev” come from?

We were inspired by Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow. The model class name draws on the distinction between fast, intuitive System 1 thinking and slow, deliberate System 2 reasoning.

“System 1 thinking” has also implied error-prone. For reasons we will get into in the future, we believe System One Models can be made more reliable than its alternatives.

We named Jev after William Stanley Jevons. We expect machine intelligence to follow a similar path to coal, after steam-engine efficiency led to an increase in demand. Every order of magnitude drop in the cost of intelligence unlocks orders of magnitude more use cases.

Why was a new training algorithm needed?

What use cases is Jev good for?

Is Jev just a smaller LLM?

How does Jev perform against public benchmarks?

Where does our training data come from?

L36:     `
L37: ##
L38: 
L39: cite5†​ L40: 
L41: Request body
L42: 
L43: The top-level shape of every request. Each entry in the `questions` map is a typed question you name.
L44: 
L45: cite6†​ L46: 
L47: [Button: state]
L48: 
L49: string | object | array
L50: 
L51: required
L52: 
L53: The content to evaluate. A plain string for text, or structured data (object/array) for things like chat logs, records, or the current state of your application. See cite7†State for formats and best practices.
L54: 
L55: cite8†​ L56: 
L57: [Button: model]
L58: 
L59: string
L60: 
L61: required
L62: The model that handles the request. Use `"jev-latest"`, TypeSafe’s flagship model. See cite9†Models for the available models and aliases.
L63: 
L64: cite10†​ L65: 
L66: [Button: questions]
L67: 
L68: map<string, Question>
L69: 
L70: required
L71: 
L72: A map of typed cite11†Question objects. You choose each key; answers come back under the same keys.
L73: 
L74: Show map entries
L75: 
L76: cite12†​ L77: 
L78: [Button: ‹question id›]
L79: 
L80: Question
L81: 
L82: A key you choose. The matching cite13†Answer is returned under this same id. The key is not sent to the underlying model and is not used in inference.
L83: Example request
L84: 
L85:     `{
L86:       "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days.",
L87:       "model": "jev-latest",
L88:       "questions": {
L89:         "is_urgent": {
L90:           "type": "noul",
L91:           "instructions": "Does this convey urgency?"
L92:         }
L93:       }
L94:     }
L95:     `
L96: ##
L97: 
L98: cite11†​ L99: 
L100: Question types
L101: 
L102: A `Question` is one of three types, set by its `type` field. All three share `type` and `instructions`; each adds its own `criteria`.
L103: ###
L104: 
L105: cite14†​ L106: 
L107: Noul
L108: 
L109: A yes/no question. Returns the probability the answer is yes.
L110: 
L111: cite15†​ L112: 
L113: [Button: type]
L114: 
L115: "noul"
L116: 
L117: required
L118: 
L119: cite16†​ L120: 
L121: [Button: instructions]
L122: 
L123: string | object | array
L124: 
L125: required
L126: 
L127: The yes/no question to evaluate.
L128: 
L129: cite17†​ L130: 
L131: [Button: criteria]
L132: 
L133: object
L134: 
L135: Optional descriptions of what a yes and a no mean.
L136: 
L137: Show properties
L138: 
L139: cite18†​ L140: 
L141: [Button: true]
L142: 
L143: string
L144: 
L145: What a yes (value near 1) means.
L146: 
L147: cite19†​ L148: 
L149: [Button: false]
L150: 
L151: string
L152: 
L153: What a no (value near 0) means.
L154: Example request
L155: 
L156:     `{
L157:       "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days.",
L158:       "model": "jev-latest",
L159:       "questions": {
L160:         "is_urgent": {
L161:           "type": "noul",
L162:           "instructions": "Does this convey urgency?",
L163:           "criteria": {
L164:             "true": "Explicitly time-sensitive",
L165:             "false": "No urgency expressed"
L166:           }
L167:         }
L168:       }
L169:     }
L170:     `
L171: ###
L172: 
L173: cite20†​ L174: 
L175: Choice
L176: 
L177: Picks one option from a set you define. Returns the chosen option and the full probability distribution.
L178: 
L179: cite21†​ L180: 
L181: [Button: type]
L182: 
L183: "choice"
L184: 
L185: required
L186: 
L187: cite22†​ L188: 
L189: [Button: instructions]
L190: 
L191: string | object | array
L192: 
L193: required
L194: 
L195: What the model should decide.
L196: 
L197: cite23†​ L198: 
L199: [Button: criteria]
L200: 
L201: map<string, string | null>
L202: 
L203: required
L204: 
L205: A map of option to rubric description; use null when an option needs no extra detail.
L206: 
L207: Show map entries
L208: 
L209: cite24†​ L210: 
L211: [Button: ‹option›]
L212: 
L213: string | null
L214: A key you choose. A description of this option.
L215: Example request
L216: 
L217:     `{
L218:       "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days.",
L219:       "model": "jev-latest",
L220:       "questions": {
L221:         "department": {
L222:           "type": "choice",
L223:           "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
L224:           "criteria": {
L225:             "billing": "Payments, invoicing, refunds",
L226:             "technical": "Bugs, outages, integrations",
L227:             "sales": "Pricing, upgrades, new accounts"
L228:           }
L229:         }
L230:       }
L231:     }
L232:     `
L233: ###
L234: 
L235: cite25†​ L236: 
L237: Score
L238: 
L239: Rates the state along a rubric you define. Returns a probability-weighted value across your levels.
L240: 
L241: cite26†​ L242: 
L243: [Button: type]
L244: 
L245: "score"
L246: 
L247: required
L248: 
L249: cite27†​ L250: 
L251: [Button: instructions]
L252: 
L253: string | object | array
L254: 
L255: required
L256: 
L257: What the model should rate.
L258: 
L259: cite28†​ L260: 
L261: [Button: criteria]
L262: 
L263: array
L264: 
L265: required
L266: 
L267: An ordered array of level descriptions. You must include at least two levels.
L268: Example request
L269: 
L270:     `{
L271:       "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days.",
L272:       "model": "jev-latest",
L273:       "questions": {
L274:         "frustration": {
L275:           "type": "score",
L276:           "instructions": "How frustrated is the customer?",
L277:           "criteria": ["Calm", "Frustrated", "Very angry"]
L278:         }
L279:       }
L280:     }
L281:     `

L284: cite29†​ L285: 
L286: Response body
L287: 
L288: One answer per question, returned under the same ids you provided.

L290: cite30†​ L291: 
L292: [Button: model]
L293: 
L294: string
L295: 
L296: required

L304: map<string, Answer>
L305: 
L306: required

L308: One cite13†Answer per question, keyed by the same ids you used in questions.

L314: [Button: ‹question id›]
L315: 
L316: Answer
L317: 
L318: The same id you chose in questions.

L356: ##
L357: 
L358: cite13†​ L359: 
L360: Answer types
L361: 
L362: Every answer carries a `type` matching its question. Choice and Score answers also carry a `confidence` between 0 to 1, derived from the answer’s probability distribution. See cite36†Confidence .

L372: 
L373: "noul"

L546: ##
L547: 
L548: cite53†​ L549: 
L550: Errors
L551: 
L552: Errors use standard HTTP status codes with a JSON body describing what went wrong.
L553: Status  | Meaning
L554: --- | ---
L555: `401 Unauthorized`  | Missing or invalid API key. Check the `Authorization` header.
L556: `422 Unprocessable Entity`  | The request body failed validation — for example a missing required field or a malformed question. The body details the offending field.
L557: `429 Too Many Requests`  | You have exceeded your rate limit. Back off and retry after a short delay.
L558: `529 Overloaded`  | TypeSafe is temporarily overloaded. Retry after a short delay.
L559: ###
L560: 
L561: cite54†​ L562: 
L563: Handling rate limits
L564: 
L565: When you receive a `429 Too Many Requests` or `529 Overloaded` response, retry the request with exponential backoff instead of retrying immediately. Our client SDKs handle this automatically, so no extra handling is needed if you use one of our SDKs with its default retry policy.

Get the details of a place based on its resource name, which is a string in the `places/{placeId}` format.

### HTTP request

`GET https://places.googleapis.com/v1/{name=places/*}`

The URL uses gRPC Transcoding syntax.

### Path parameters

Parameters
---
`name`  | `string` Required. The resource name of a place, in the `places/{placeId}` format.

### Query parameters

Parameters
---
`languageCode`  | `string` Optional. Place details will be displayed with the preferred language if available.Current list of supported languages: https://developers.google.com/maps/faq#languagesupport.
`regionCode`  | `string` Optional. The Unicode country/region code (CLDR) of the location where the request is coming from. This parameter is used to display the place details, like region-specific place name, if available. The parameter can affect results based on applicable law. For more information, see https://www.unicode.org/cldr/charts/latest/supplemental/territory_language_information.html.Note that 3-digit region codes are not currently supported.
`sessionToken`  | `string` Optional. A string which identifies an Autocomplete session for billing purposes. Must be a URL and filename safe base64 string with at most 36 ASCII characters in length. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Q: What does the API response look like if a review response gets removed by the user natively?
A: Deleted review won’t show up in the API response, but you do get a webhook for it.

Q: Are the reactions to reviews: “Useful”, “Funny”, “Cool” available via API?
A: No, not today.

Q: Does Yelp API support deleting existing reviews?
A: We don’t support any deletion of reviews left by consumers, except if the consumer deletes it themselves. Business owners' responses to reviews can be removed but they have to do so via logging into biz.yelp.com. This isn’t supported by an API today.

Fusion API and Related Data

Q: I see this note in the ‘business details’ endpoint “Note: at this time, the API does not return businesses without any reviews.” Can we get an exception to this behavior?
A: Request this via [email protected].

Q: The “Get Businesses Associated with Access Token” endpoint returns business ids. Do we need to use the Fusion API and request business details for each one? Is there a way to make a single request for a batch of business ids?
A: Via the Fusion API: you’d use the business details endpoint to query more info about each returned id. These requests are done 1 biz id at a time. We can set a rate limit that allows you to process these requests in bulk. OR we can set you up with access to the GraphQL endpoint.

Q: We have noticed that the images url on Fusion API end with “o.png”, we may need other sizes, is this supported?
A: Yes, you can change that “o”, other accepted options are l,ls,m,s,xs,ls,ms,ss, & xss

Q: Can we have access to page rankings on Yelp?
A: Not exactly, via the Reporting API we give raw metrics like clicks/views, but we don’t expose the equivalent % rank for the location’s cat/geo.

content.text:
Yes, Girl Dinner is a strong fit for Jev. The key is that Jev will make the judgment; it will not discover restaurants or fetch menus itself. We supply the current people, preferences, locations, and restaurant data as structured state, and Jev returns typed scores and probabilities that our code can rank.

### 1. How we’ll use Jev

Jev accepts:

- A `state`: text or structured JSON containing everything it should consider.
- One or more typed questions.
- The `jev-latest` model.

It supports three question types:

- **Score**: Rate something on levels we define.
- **Choice**: Select from a fixed set of options.
- **Noul**: Return the probability that a yes/no statement is true.

The response is structured data rather than generated prose. Score and Choice answers include probability distributions and confidence values. Questions sharing the same state can be evaluated together in one request. [Jev introduction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction), [question primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives), [API reference](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api).

For Girl Dinner, the flow should look like this:

1. Each person supplies cravings, dislikes, dietary restrictions, budget, travel preference, and location.
2. Normal code finds nearby restaurants and calculates distances or travel times.
3. We remove restaurants that fail hard rules such as being closed, too far away, or having no verified option for an allergy.
4. We send the remaining restaurants and party preferences to Jev.
5. Jev independently scores each restaurant against each person’s preferences and the overall group.
6. Our code combines those scores, accounting for both the average and the least-satisfied person.
7. If the top result has low confidence or two restaurants are nearly tied, Girl Dinner asks one focused follow-up question.

A simplified state would resemble:

```json
{
  "people": [
    {
      "id": "alex",
      "cravings": ["spicy", "noodles"],
      "dietaryRestrictions": ["vegetarian"],
      "budget": "$$"
    },
    {
      "id": "sam",
      "cravings": ["Thai", "something light"],
      "dietaryRestrictions": [],
      "budget": "$$"
    }
  ],
  "restaurants": [
    {
      "id": "restaurant_123",
      "cuisines": ["Thai"],
      "priceLevel": 2,
      "openNow": true,
      "travelMinutes": {
        "alex": 12,
        "sam": 9
      },
      "menuItems": [
        {
          "name": "Vegetable drunken noodles",
          "tags": ["vegetarian", "spicy"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

We would send narrow Score questions such as:

- How well does restaurant 123 match Alex’s current cravings?
- How well does restaurant 123 match Sam’s current cravings?
- How much appealing menu variety does restaurant 123 offer this party?
- How well does restaurant 123 fit the party’s requested dining experience?

Our code would normalize those answers and calculate a final rank. Jev’s documentation specifically recommends splitting broad judgments into atomic questions, asking them together, and combining their outputs in code. [How to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one).

Dietary allergies should be enforced as hard application rules using explicit menu or allergen data. Jev can help interpret fuzzy descriptions such as “something light,” but it should not be the final authority on whether a meal is medically safe.

For confidence, we can use a product behavior like:

- High confidence: show the recommendation.
- Medium confidence: show two finalists or ask one tie-breaking question.
- Low confidence: ask for more preference information.

That follows TypeSafe’s recommended confidence-gated approach. [Confidence documentation](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence).

For implementation, TypeSafe provides an official JavaScript/TypeScript SDK:

```bash
npm install @typesafe-ai/sdk
```

It requires Node.js 20 or newer, reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from the environment, and uses `jev-latest` by default. [Official JavaScript SDK](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-sdk-js).

### 2. What I need from you

The only credential we definitely need for Jev is a **TypeSafe API key**. It is not currently available in this workspace.

You’ll need to:

1. Sign in to the [TypeSafe console](https://console.typesafe.ai/settings/keys).
2. Create an API key.
3. Add it to the project as `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`.

Please don’t paste the key into chat or commit it to Git. Once we choose the application framework, we’ll put it in the appropriate local environment file and ensure that file is ignored. The key must stay on the server; the browser should call our server endpoint rather than TypeSafe directly.

I cannot independently generate that key because it belongs to your TypeSafe account and may involve login, accepting their terms, credits, or billing. I can handle all code and configuration after it has been provisioned.

For the complete product, we will probably also need:

- **Google Maps/Places credentials** for restaurant discovery, place details, maps, and possibly travel times. Google requires a Cloud project, an API key, enabled APIs, and billing. Nearby Search can return restaurants, locations, cuisine types, price information, ratings, hours, websites, and some dining attributes. [Google Places Nearby Search](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/nearby-search).
- **No key for device GPS itself.** Web browsers expose location through `navigator.geolocation`; each participant must grant permission. It requires HTTPS in production. [Browser geolocation guidance](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/javascript/geolocation).
- **A menu-data strategy.** Google Places does not provide complete structured restaurant menus. It can provide the restaurant website and some attributes, but not dependable item-by-item menu and allergen data. Yelp’s paid Places plans can provide a menu URL, but that still is not necessarily a structured menu feed. [Google Place fields](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/reference/rest/v1/places), [Yelp plan fields](https://docs.developer.yelp.com/page/start-your-free-trial).

My recommendation is to begin with Google Places for discovery and use restaurant metadata plus sample structured menus while we prove the Jev scoring workflow. Then we can choose a production menu source based on target launch cities and budget.

So, the immediate requirement from you is the TypeSafe API key. We can build the interface, data model, scoring architecture, and mocked restaurant flow before the Google key or menu provider is ready.
oh last requirement if no decision is made then we can decide that they need to eat a girl dinner..which could be just make a light plate at home..and give them suggestions for that.

That becomes the app’s signature fallback: when the group cannot settle on a restaurant, Girl Dinner recommends an easy light plate at home.

“No decision” can mean:

- No restaurant satisfies everyone’s hard requirements.
- Jev’s confidence is too low.
- The leading options are effectively tied.
- Everyone rejects the recommendations.
- The group reaches a time or voting limit.

The fallback can assemble a plate from a curated catalog:

- Something savory: cheese, hummus, deli meat, olives
- Something crunchy: crackers, toast, chips, cucumbers
- Produce: fruit, tomatoes, carrots
- Something filling: eggs, tuna, beans, yogurt
- A treat: chocolate, cookies, dates
- An optional drink

Because Jev chooses from supplied options rather than generating new text, we’ll give it eligible ingredients or preset plates and have it score them against cravings, dietary restrictions, preparation time, and what people have at home. If users enter their available ingredients, it can recommend a personalized plate; otherwise, the app can offer a few broadly available combinations.

For groups, we can recommend either one shared board or individual mini plates. Allergies and dietary restrictions will remain hard filters in code.

A result might read:

> No restaurant won tonight. It’s Girl Dinner time: hummus, warm pita, cucumbers, olives, grapes, and a little chocolate. Ready in 8 minutes.

I’ll treat this as a core outcome alongside restaurant recommendations, rather than merely an error state.
